lesson.title: Safe Wi-Fi
lesson.subtitle: At school, at home and in town

video.title: Safe Wi-Fi
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds; narration in the lesson language, captions as separate files.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A busy café. Farah marks papers with her phone beside her; a Wi-Fi sign on the wall reads “Free Wi-Fi”. Other customers sit at nearby tables, phones out.
scenes.animation: Wi-Fi waves pulse from the sign; Farah glances around.
scenes.narration: I’m marking at a café, on the free Wi-Fi. I’ve just signed in to the school portal. Should I worry about who else is on this network?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: what others can see on Wi-Fi, and how to set up yours safely.

scenes.visual: Two message envelopes travel from a phone through the café router. One is open, its words readable; the other is sealed with a padlock, only the website’s name on the outside.
scenes.animation: Envelopes slide along the line; the open one’s words float up.
scenes.narration: Whoever runs a Wi-Fi network can see which websites your phone visits. With a plain HTTP page, which your browser marks “Not secure”, they can read everything you send. With HTTPS, the padlock, what’s inside is scrambled: they see the website’s name, but not your password or your marks.

scenes.visual: A phone’s Wi-Fi list shows two near-identical names. Behind one, a man with a laptop in a backpack; a fake sign-in page pops up on the phone.
scenes.animation: The list scrolls; the fake page slides up.
scenes.narration: And here’s the catch. Anyone can set up a hotspot and call it “Free Bus Station WiFi”. A fake hotspot sees everything a real one sees, and it may show you a fake sign-in page. A name on a list proves nothing.

scenes.visual: Clean card in two halves: on the left, a phone reading news on Wi-Fi; on the right, the same phone switched to mobile data for a mobile money payment and an email.
scenes.animation: A toggle flips from Wi-Fi to mobile data.
scenes.narration: So here’s the rule. On public Wi-Fi, read the news or watch a video: that’s fine. But for mobile money, banking, email and pupils’ marks, switch to mobile data. And turn off auto-join, so your phone doesn’t connect by itself to any network with a familiar name.

scenes.visual: Farah at a bus station, holding her phone with two network names on screen. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check. I need to pay a bill with mobile money at the bus station. I can see “Bus Station Free” and “Bus Station Free WiFi”. Which one should I use?

scenes.visual: The “neither” card gets the check badge. The phone switches to mobile data; a signal line runs straight to a phone company mast.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the signal line draws to the mast.
scenes.narration: Neither. For money, switch to mobile data, which goes straight to your phone company. A few megabytes of data cost far less than an emptied mobile money account.

scenes.visual: A tunnel runs from the phone through the café router to a building labelled “VPN company”, then on to the website. The café owner sees only the tunnel; a window in the VPN building shows everything.
scenes.animation: The tunnel draws itself; a small eye opens in the VPN building.
scenes.narration: What about a VPN? A VPN wraps your traffic in a tunnel, so the café owner sees nothing but the tunnel. But the VPN company can see it all instead. So avoid unknown free VPN apps: if it’s free, your data may be what it sells.

scenes.visual: A home router on a shelf. A sticky note “admin / admin” is crossed out; a settings page shows WPA3 selected and a long password; an update arrow spins.
scenes.animation: The sticky note is crossed out; settings tick on one by one.
scenes.narration: Now your own Wi-Fi, at home or at school. Change the router’s admin password, because the one it came with is often easy to find or guess. Choose WPA2 or WPA3 security, with a long Wi-Fi password. And update the router, just like your phone.

scenes.visual: A school plan: a guest network bubble around the hall and classrooms, a separate bubble around the office with the records cabinet. A Wi-Fi password written on a classroom wall gets wiped off.
scenes.animation: The two bubbles draw separately; the wall writing is wiped.
scenes.narration: At school, give visitors and pupils a guest network. Keep the office computers, with the records, on a separate network. And don’t write the Wi-Fi password on the classroom wall. If you share your phone’s hotspot, give it a password, and switch it off when you’re done.

scenes.visual: Joseph beside a new router in the school office, its box on the desk. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our new school router still uses the admin password it came with. Is that safe to leave?

scenes.visual: The “change it” card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: HTTPS · Mobile data · Router · Guest network
scenes.narration: No: change it, because the passwords routers come with are often easy to find or guess. Remember: HTTPS hides what’s inside, a network’s name proves nothing, money goes over mobile data, and your router gets a new password, WPA2 or WPA3, and updates.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. On the board: a café, a phone and a website joined by lines. Pupils add envelopes, some open, some sealed with padlocks.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: draw a café, a phone and a website on the board. Pupils draw what travels between them, and mark what the café owner can see, with and without the padlock.

checkpoints.prompt: At the bus station you need to pay a bill with mobile money. Two free networks have almost the same name. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the one with the stronger signal
Try both and use the one that works
Use neither: switch to mobile data

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: anyone can name a network. Money goes over mobile data.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a strong signal or a working connection doesn’t prove a network is real. Use mobile data for money.

checkpoints.prompt: The new school router still uses the admin password it came with. Safe to leave it?

options.text: Yes: only staff ever see the router
No: change it, because default passwords are easy to find

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the passwords routers come with are often easy to find or guess. Change it today.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: anyone on the network can try the password the router came with. Change it.
